title: 01. Fundamentals & Trade-offs: PACELC Theorem
summary: PACELC (pronounced "pack-elk"), formulated by Daniel Abadi in 2010, extends CAP: if a Partition (P) occurs, the system chooses between Availability (A) and Consistency (C); Else (E), when operating normally, it chooses between…
objectives: State PACELC and explain what it adds beyond CAP.
Classify Cassandra, Spanner, and default MongoDB into PACELC buckets.
Why does strong consistency (EC) cost latency in normal operation?
Is it possible for a system to be PA/EC? What would that look like, and why is it rare?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** PACELC (pronounced "pack-elk"), formulated by Daniel Abadi in 2010, extends CAP: **if a Partition (P) occurs, the system chooses between Availability (A) and Consistency (C); Else (E), when operating normally, it chooses between Latency (L) and Consistency (C)** — written as `PA/EL`, `PC/EC`, `PA/EC`, or `PC/EL`.

CAP tells you what happens during a partition — but most systems spend the vast majority of their time *not* partitioned. What trade-off do they make in normal operation? That is the question PACELC answers. The acronym unpacks as: **P**artition → **A**vailability vs **C**onsistency; **E**lse → **L**atency vs **C**onsistency. Every distributed database can be classified into one of four PACELC buckets. **PA/EL** systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak) choose availability under partition *and* low latency over consistency in normal operation — they are the "always fast, always writable" family. **PC/EC** systems (Spanner, MongoDB with majority writes, HBase) choose consistency under partition *and* pay the latency cost of synchronous coordination in normal operation. **PA/EC** is rare but exists — systems that pick availability under partition but impose synchronous coordination in normal operation (VoltDB is sometimes classified here, depending on configuration). **PC/EL** is also rare — PNUTS, the Yahoo system from which the original Abadi analysis drew, picks consistency under partition but favors low latency (eventual consistency between regions) in normal operation.

Why does PACELC matter? Because the *normal-operation* trade-off is what your users feel every day. CAP availability matters only during the rare partition window; PACELC latency matters on every single request. If you pick a PC/EC system like Spanner, you pay 5–10 ms of cross-region Paxos round-trip on every write — that is the price of strong consistency. If you pick a PA/EL system like Cassandra, every write returns in <1 ms but reads may briefly return stale data. Users notice the latency long before they notice a partition.

The canonical real-world example is **Cassandra vs. Spanner**. Cassandra is PA/EL: it accepts writes on any replica during a partition (PA), and in normal operation uses its tunable consistency at `ONE` to return writes in under a millisecond (EL) — sacrificing strong consistency in exchange. This is why Netflix, Instagram, and Apple use Cassandra for time-series and user-data workloads where write latency is critical. Google Spanner is PC/EC: it uses Paxos across datacenters to refuse writes that cannot reach quorum during a partition (PC), and in normal operation every write commits through a Paxos round plus a TrueTime commit-wait window of ~5–7 ms (EC). Spanner's users — Google AdWords, Google Play, and external Spanner customers — accept the latency because they need cross-region strong consistency. The same workload moved from one to the other would feel completely different to users.

**MongoDB** is an interesting case. With default settings, MongoDB is *PC/EL-ish*: writes go to the primary's oplog and are replicated to secondaries asynchronously, so under partition the primary on the minority side steps down (PC), but in normal operation writes return as soon as the primary applies them locally (EL — low latency). With `writeConcern: {w: "majority"}`, MongoDB becomes PC/EC: writes must be acknowledged by a majority, paying a synchronous replication round-trip in normal operation. This is a beautiful illustration of PACELC's power: the *same* database can shift its PACELC class based on configuration, and the engineer's job is to pick the right config for the workload.

A common pitfall is **ignoring the latency penalty** of strong consistency. Engineers sometimes default to "stronger is safer" — they set all Cassandra reads to `ALL` or all Mongo writes to `{w: "majority", j: true}` — and then are surprised when p99 latency triples. The synchronous coordination cost is real: every extra replica acknowledgment is a network round-trip, often across an AZ boundary. PACELC makes this cost visible and explicit. The rule of thumb: only pay for the consistency your application actually needs, on the operations that actually need it. Netflix's Cassandra deployment mixes `LOCAL_ONE` for time-series reads (fast, stale OK) with `LOCAL_QUORUM` for billing-critical writes (slower, consistent).

Another pitfall is **treating PACELC as a marketing label**. Vendors sometimes claim "PA/EL" without justifying it. The right test is empirical: under partition, does the system return errors (PC) or accept writes (PA)? In normal operation, does a write block on multi-node acknowledgment (EC) or return after local application (EL)? Run the experiment; do not trust the brochure.

A second real-world illustration is **YouTube's view-count pipeline**, which combines PACELC classes for different stages. The view event itself is written to a Kafka log (high throughput, eventual consistency — effectively EL on the ingestion path). A stream processor aggregates views per video and writes the running total to a Cassandra cluster at `LOCAL_ONE` (PA/EL) — viewers tolerate a stale count by a few seconds, and the write volume is too high to pay quorum latency. A separate batch job periodically writes the reconciled count to a Spanner-backed analytics dashboard (PC/EC) where finance teams need accurate, audit-grade numbers. The same business concept — "view count" — flows through three different PACELC classes depending on the consumer's consistency and latency needs. This is the modern data-engineering pattern: pick the PACELC class per pipeline stage, not per database.

A useful mental model is to think of PACELC as a *cost*: every "C" you add (PC instead of PA, or EC instead of EL) costs you something — availability under partition or latency in normal operation. A well-designed system pays this cost only where the business actually needs it, and accepts the cheaper "A" or "L" choice everywhere else. The mistake is to either pay everywhere (over-consistent, slow, expensive) or nowhere (under-consistent, fast, but correctness bugs in production). The senior engineer's job is to know exactly which operations are in which bucket and to defend that classification against both "make it safer" and "make it faster" pressures.

PACELC connects to nearly every concept in this phase. It refines **CAP** (Topic 10) by adding the no-partition case. It quantifies the **latency** (Topic 8) cost of **consistency**. It explains why **throughput** (Topic 9) drops when you raise consistency: synchronous coordination reduces concurrency. It is the underlying reason **durability** (Topic 6) and **reliability** (Topic 5) trade off against latency. And it is the conceptual foundation for choosing between **vertical scaling** (Topic 12) — packing more on one box to avoid coordination — versus **horizontal scaling** — spreading across boxes and accepting PACELC trade-offs.

```mermaid
    PQ -->|Availability| PA[PA: accept writes on both sides]
    PQ -->|Consistency| PC[PC: refuse writes without quorum]

    Q -->|No - E| EQ{Choose L or C}
    EQ -->|Latency| EL[EL: local ack, return fast]
    EQ -->|Consistency| EC[EC: wait for quorum ack]

    PA --> PAEL[Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak = PA/EL]

    style PAEL fill:#cfc,stroke:#060
    style PCEC fill:#fcc,stroke:#600
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
                 PACELC = CAP + (Else --> Latency vs Consistency)
                              +-------------------+
                              |  Normal Operation |
                              |  (no partition)   |
                              |                   |
                  +-----------|   Else (E)        |
                  |           |   L  vs  C        |
                  |           +-------------------+
                  |
   +--------------+---------------+
   |       Distributed System     |
   +--------------+---------------+
                  |
                  |           +-------------------+
                  +---------->|   Partition (P)   |
                              |   A  vs  C        |
                              +-------------------+

   Classification table:
   +--------+---------------+-------------------------------------+
   | PACELC | Under P       | Under E (normal)                    |
   +--------+---------------+-------------------------------------+
   | PA/EL  | Accept writes | Local ack, low latency              |
   | PA/EC  | Accept writes | Wait quorum, high latency           |
   | PC/EL  | Refuse writes | Local ack, low latency              |
   | PC/EC  | Refuse writes | Wait quorum, high latency           |
   +--------+---------------+-------------------------------------+

   Examples:
     PA/EL : Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak, Couchbase
     PC/EC : Spanner, MongoDB (majority), HBase, etcd
     PC/EL : PNUTS (Yahoo), MongoDB (default w:1)
     PA/EC : rare - configured VoltDB
```

### Walkthrough
1. Start with a distributed system and ask the first question: **is there a network partition right now?** This is the "P" branch. If yes, the system must choose between Availability (accept writes on all sides, reconcile later) and Consistency (refuse writes that cannot reach quorum).
2. If there is no partition (the "Else" branch), the system is in normal operation and must choose between Latency (return after local application — fast but stale-prone) and Consistency (wait for a quorum of replicas to acknowledge — slower but strongly consistent).
3. Combine the two choices to classify the system: PA/EL (Cassandra), PA/EC (rare), PC/EL (MongoDB default, PNUTS), or PC/EC (Spanner, MongoDB with majority writes). The classification determines what users feel during partitions *and* on every normal request.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- PACELC classifier.
- Build the PACELC label: P? → A or C (under partition) E? → L or C (in normal operation) Returns e.g. 'PA/EL', 'PC/EC', 'PA/EC', 'PC/EL'
- Reference catalog of well-known systems

**Defines:** `SystemBehavior`, `pacelc_classify()`, `explain()`

```python
"""
PACELC classifier.
Given a system's behavior under partition and in normal operation, output its PACELC class.
Also classify well-known systems as a reference table.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List

@dataclass
class SystemBehavior:
    name: str
    partition_choice: str          # 'A' or 'C'
    normal_choice: str             # 'L' or 'C'

def pacelc_classify(behavior: SystemBehavior) -> str:
    """
    Build the PACELC label:
      P?  → A or C  (under partition)
      E?  → L or C  (in normal operation)
    Returns e.g. 'PA/EL', 'PC/EC', 'PA/EC', 'PC/EL'
    """
    p = behavior.partition_choice.upper()
    e = behavior.normal_choice.upper()
    if p not in ("A", "C"):
        raise ValueError(f"partition_choice must be 'A' or 'C', got {p}")
    if e not in ("L", "C"):
        raise ValueError(f"normal_choice must be 'L' or 'C', got {e}")
    return f"P{p}/E{e}"

def explain(label: str) -> str:
    table = {
        "PA/EL": "Always available, always fast — accepts writes on any replica during partition; "
                 "in normal operation, acks locally with low latency. Trades consistency. "
                 "Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak.",
        "PA/EC": "Available during partition, but pays for strong consistency in normal operation. "
                 "Rare; some VoltDB configurations. Accepts writes during partition but waits for "
                 "quorum ack normally.",
        "PC/EL": "Refuses writes during partition (CP-style), but in normal operation returns fast "
                 "after local ack. Examples: PNUTS, MongoDB with default w:1 writes.",
        "PC/EC": "Strong consistency always: refuses writes during partition and waits for quorum "
                 "in normal operation. Pays latency for consistency. Examples: Spanner, MongoDB "
                 "with w:majority, etcd.",
    }
    return table.get(label, "Unknown PACELC class")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Reference catalog of well-known systems
    systems = [
        SystemBehavior("Cassandra (CL=ONE)",          partition_choice="A", normal_choice="L"),
        SystemBehavior("Cassandra (CL=QUORUM)",       partition_choice="A", normal_choice="C"),
        SystemBehavior("DynamoDB (eventual reads)",   partition_choice="A", normal_choice="L"),
        SystemBehavior("DynamoDB (strong reads)",     partition_choice="A", normal_choice="C"),
        SystemBehavior("MongoDB (w:1 default)",       partition_choice="C", normal_choice="L"),
        SystemBehavior("MongoDB (w:majority)",        partition_choice="C", normal_choice="C"),
        SystemBehavior("Google Spanner",              partition_choice="C", normal_choice="C"),
        SystemBehavior("etcd (Raft)",                 partition_choice="C", normal_choice="C"),
        SystemBehavior("HBase (HDFS quorum)",         partition_choice="C", normal_choice="C"),
        SystemBehavior("Riak (default)",              partition_choice="A", normal_choice="L"),
        SystemBehavior("PNUTS",                       partition_choice="C", normal_choice="L"),
        SystemBehavior("VoltDB (some configs)",       partition_choice="A", normal_choice="C"),
    ]

    print(f"{'System':<32} {'Partition':>10} {'Normal':>8} {'PACELC':>8}")
    print("-" * 64)
    for s in systems:
        label = pacelc_classify(s)
        print(f"{s.name:<32} {s.partition_choice:>10} {s.normal_choice:>8} {label:>8}")

    print("\n--- Detail for the canonical four buckets ---")
    canonical = [
        SystemBehavior("Cassandra-default", partition_choice="A", normal_choice="L"),
        SystemBehavior("Spanner",           partition_choice="C", normal_choice="C"),
        SystemBehavior("MongoDB-default",   partition_choice="C", normal_choice="L"),
        SystemBehavior("VoltDB-config",     partition_choice="A", normal_choice="C"),
    ]
    for s in canonical:
        label = pacelc_classify(s)
        print(f"\n{s.name} → {label}")
        print(f"  {explain(label)}")
```

quiz.explanation: PACELC says: in a distributed system, if a Partition (P) occurs, choose between Availability (A) and Consistency (C); Else (E), in normal operation, choose between Latency (L) and Consistency (C). It adds the "else" branch that CAP omits. CAP only tells you what happens during a partition — but partitions are rare.

quiz.explanation: Strong consistency in a distributed system requires that a write be acknowledged by a quorum of replicas before the coordinator returns success — this is the only way to guarantee that subsequent reads (also touching a quorum) will see the write, by the quorum intersection property. Each replica acknowledgment is a network round-trip, often across an AZ boundary (1–2 ms in a single region, 30–100 ms across regions).

This is unusual because the two choices seem contradictory — if you care enough about consistency to pay quorum latency in normal operation, why accept divergent writes during partitions?
